claim: More than 250 million individuals worldwide are chronic HBV carriers
source: As a result, more than 250 million individuals worldwide are chronic HBV carriers (Plummer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Plummer et al., 2016

claim: NK cells are activated during acute HBV infection before the onset of adaptive immunity
source: In patients, NK cells are activated during acute HBV infection before the onset of adaptive immunity (Dunn et al., 2009; Fisicaro et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2012; Lunemann et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: NK cells from CHB patients are characterised by a decreased capacity to produce cytokines such as IFN-γ and TNF-α despite maintaining or even increasing their cytotoxic capacity
source: Indeed, NK cells from CHB patients are characterised by a decreased capacity to produce cytokines such as IFN-γ and TNF-α despite maintaining or even increasing their cytotoxic capacity (Oliviero et al., 2009; Peppa et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2012; Tjwa et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple published studies

claim: The phenomenon of decreased cytokine production with maintained cytotoxicity in CHB patient NK cells has been termed 'functional dichotomy'
source: This phenomenon has been termed 'functional dichotomy' (Oliviero et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oliviero et al., 2009

claim: A decrease in the expression of several activating receptors was previously observed in CHB patient's NK cells
source: In HBV-infected patients, this balance might be skewed as a decrease in the expression of several activating receptors was previously observed in patient's NK cells (Lunemann et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2012; Tjwa et al., 2011; Heiberg et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple published studies

claim: NK cells from CHB patients with high viral loads or liver damage display increased expression of certain inhibitory receptors including NKG2A and TIM3
source: Furthermore, NK cells from CHB patients with high viral loads or liver damage display increased expression of certain inhibitory receptors including immune-checkpoint (ICP) markers such as NKG2A or T cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain containing 3 (TIM3) (Ju et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The mTOR pathway integrates positive and negative signals derived from cytokines such as IL-15, IL-12, or TGF-β to control NK cell metabolism and functions
source: Molecularly, we and others have shown that the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway integrates positive and negative signals derived from cytokines such as IL-15, IL-12, or TGF-β, respectively, to control NK cell metabolism and functions (Marçais et al., 2014; Viel et al., 2016; Marçais et al., 2017; Donnelly et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple published studies including authors' own work

claim: Immuno-modulatory cytokines such as IL-10 and TGF-β are involved in the emergence/maintenance of the dysfunctional NK cell phenotype in CHB
source: In the context of CHB, reports also involved immuno-modulatory cytokines such as IL-10 and TGF-β in the emergence/maintenance of the dysfunctional phenotype (Peppa et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2012; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: T cell exhaustion has been defined as a stepwise differentiation process arising in situations of chronic stimulation
source: Indeed, T cell exhaustion has been defined as a stepwise differentiation process arising in situations of chronic stimulation and combining (1) a gradual loss of effector functions and proliferative capacities, (2) an altered metabolism, (3) the expression of defined ICP functioning as inhibitory receptors, and (4) a specific transcriptional and epigenetic program (McLane et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to McLane et al., 2019

claim: The transcription factors responsible for the appearance of the exhausted phenotype in T cells include NFAT, TOX, and NR4A family members
source: The transcription factors responsible for the appearance of the exhausted phenotype in T cells have recently been identified and include NFAT, TOX, and NR4A family members (Martinez et al., 2015; Khan et al., 2019; Seo et al., 2019; Alfei et al., 2019; Scott et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple published studies

claim: NFAT activation results from unbalanced signalling due to defective co-stimulation leading to preferential activation of the signalling branch dependent on Ca2+ flux
source: Mechanistically, it was proposed that NFAT activation resulted from unbalanced signalling due to defective co-stimulation leading to preferential activation of the signalling branch dependent on Ca2+ flux (Martinez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martinez et al., 2015

claim: NFAT drives the expression of TOX and NR4As in exhausted T cells
source: NFAT would then behave as an initiating transcription factor by further driving the expression of TOX and NR4As (Seo et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The 32 patients constituting the study cohort are in the immune inactive phase characterised by persistent HBV infection of the liver, absence of significant necroinflammatory disease, low serum HBV DNA levels, and normal serum aminotransferases
source: The 32 patients constituting our cohort are in the immune inactive phase characterised by persistent HBV infection of the liver, absence of significant necroinflammatory disease (data not shown), low serum HBV DNA levels, and normal serum aminotransferases.
evidence: Supported by clinical data from the study cohort presented in Table 1

claim: A higher proportion of CHB patients than HD were seropositive for Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV)
source: Similar to previously described cohorts, a higher proportion of CHB patients than HD were seropositive for Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV) (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Higher HCMV seropositivity in CHB patients led to higher representation of the adaptive NKG2C+ subset in the NK cell population
source: a characteristic that led to higher representation of the adaptive NKG2C+ subset in the NK cell population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: NK cells of CHB patients exhibited normal degranulation in response to K562 stimulation
source: As shown in Figure 1A, NK cells of CHB patients exhibited normal degranulation in response to K562 stimulation.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Basal levels of CD107a were increased in NK cells from CHB patients suggestive of recent stimulation
source: Yet, basal levels of CD107a were increased in NK cells from CHB patients suggestive of recent stimulation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased basal CD107a levels

claim: The cytotoxic capacity of NK cells was not affected by HBV infection
source: As shown in Figure 1B, the cytotoxic capacity of NK cells was not affected by HBV infection.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B measuring direct cytotoxicity against K562 cells

claim: A significantly decreased capacity to produce IFN-γ and MIP1-β upon K562 stimulation was observed in CHB patient NK cells
source: In contrast, a significantly decreased capacity to produce IFN-γ and MIP1-β upon K562 stimulation was observed (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C

claim: TNF-α secretion capacity was decreased and tightly correlated with the decrease in IFN-γ secretion capacity in CHB patient NK cells
source: TNF-α secretion capacity was also decreased and tightly correlated with the decrease in IFN-γ secretion capacity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A); however, this decrease did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: Degranulation in response to Rituximab-coated Granta cells was normal in CHB patients
source: Degranulation was normal in CHB patients as measured by CD107a surface exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B

claim: IFN-γ production was decreased in CHB patient NK cells in response to Rituximab-coated Granta cells
source: while IFN-γ production was decreased (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The overall percentage of NK cells was decreased in CHB patients
source: We observed that the overall percentage of NK cells was decreased in CHB patients, but this did not impact the relative representation of CD56bright vs CD56dim subsets (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The relative representation of CD56bright vs CD56dim subsets was not impacted in CHB patients
source: We observed that the overall percentage of NK cells was decreased in CHB patients, but this did not impact the relative representation of CD56bright vs CD56dim subsets (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The expression of activating receptors CD16 and NKp30 was significantly decreased in CHB patients
source: The expression of activating receptors CD16 and NKp30 was significantly decreased, while that of NKG2D was increased in CHB patients (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The expression of NKG2D was increased in CHB patients
source: The expression of activating receptors CD16 and NKp30 was significantly decreased, while that of NKG2D was increased in CHB patients (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The expression of NKp46 and DNAM activating receptors was not statistically different between HD and CHB patients
source: the expression of NKp46 and DNAM activating receptors was not statistically different between HD and patients (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: An overall reduction in the expression of the inhibitory receptors CD160, KLRG1, and NKG2A was observed in CHB patients
source: We also observed an overall reduction in the expression of the inhibitory receptors CD160, KLRG1, and NKG2A (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The reduction in inhibitory receptor expression was statistically significant only for CD160
source: However, this variation was statistically significant only for CD160.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The changes in NKp30, CD16, NKG2D, and CD160 expression were restricted to the CD56Dim subset
source: Of note, the changes we observed for NKp30, CD16, NKG2D, and CD160 were restricted to the CD56Dim subset (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: No difference was detected in the expression of Perforin and Granzyme B in NK cells of CHB patients compared to HD
source: We did not detect any difference in the expression of these molecules nor in total NK cells neither in the CD56Dim/Bright subsets in accordance with the fact that cytotoxic capacities are preserved (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: Basal levels of pS6 and pAKT were decreased in total and CD56Dim NK cells of CHB patients compared to HD
source: As depicted in Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C, basal levels of pS6 and pAKT were decreased in total and CD56Dim, but not CD56Bright NK cells of CHB patients compared to HD
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: Basal pSTAT5 levels were not affected in CHB patient NK cells
source: while pSTAT5 levels were not affected.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Basal or IL-15-induced levels of pS6 were correlated to IFN-γ production in CHB patients
source: Of note, when focusing on CHB patients, we found that basal or IL-15-induced levels of pS6 were correlated to IFN-γ production, so that patients with low pS6 also showed low IFN-γ production (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: mTOR activation was lower in total NK cells from CHB patients than in NK cells from HD upon IL-15 stimulation
source: Upon IL-15 stimulation, mTOR activation was lower in total NK cells from CHB patients than in NK cells from HD as shown by the decreased phosphorylation of both S6 and AKT (p-values of 0.11 and 0.038, respectively).
evidence: Supported by data showing decreased phosphorylation of S6 and AKT

claim: Both pS6 and pAKT phosphorylations were reduced in CD56bright NK cells from CHB patients upon IL-15 stimulation
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, both phosphorylations were reduced in CHB patients upon IL-15 stimulation.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: IL-15 triggering of pSTAT5 was not affected in CHB patient NK cells
source: This defective induction was specific to the mTOR pathway as IL-15 triggering of pSTAT5 was not affected (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: Circulating TGF-β1 levels were significantly higher in CHB patients
source: Circulating TGF-β1 levels were indeed significantly higher in CHB patients (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B

claim: No correlation was observed between TGF-β1 concentration and pS6 level in the CHB patient group
source: However, no correlation was observed between TGF-β1 concentration and pS6 level neither at basal nor after IL-15 stimulation in the CHB patient group (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by analysis of the data

claim: NK cell size was not affected in CHB patients
source: As shown in Figure 3C, NK cell size was not affected in CHB patients (forward scatter [FSC] parameter)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C

claim: NK cells from CHB patients presented decreased granularity
source: while they presented decreased granularity (side scatter [SSC] parameter).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C

claim: CD98 and CD71 were expressed at equivalent levels at basal state and their induction by IL-15 was normal in CHB patient NK cells
source: Furthermore, two nutrient transporters regulated by mTOR (Marçais et al., 2014), the heavy chain of system L amino-acid transporter (CD98) and the transferrin transporter (CD71), were also expressed at equivalent levels at basal state and their induction by IL-15 was normal (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D,E

claim: Normal functionality of the system L amino-acid transporter was confirmed in both HD and CHB patients as measured by the uptake of kynurenine
source: Normal functionality of the system L amino-acid transporter was confirmed in both HD and CHB patients as measured by the uptake of kynurenine (Sinclair et al., 2018), a fluorescent derivative of tryptophan carried by the system L transporter (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3F

claim: No change in global mitochondrial mass or mitochondrial production of ROS was observed between HD and CHB patient NK cells
source: Hence, we quantified the global mitochondrial mass using the Mitotracker dye, and mitochondrial production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) using the MitoSOX dye, yet we did not observe any change between the two groups nor at basal state neither after IL-15 stimulation (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Principal component analysis of RNAseq results showed a clear separation between HD and CHB patients on PC1 and 2, with 38% and 24% variance, respectively
source: As shown in Figure 4A, principal component analysis (PCA) of the results showed a clear separation between HD and CHB patients both on PC1 and 2, with 38% and 24% variance, respectively
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A

claim: 253 genes were up-regulated and 163 genes were down-regulated specific to HBV infection in CHB patients after filtering out genes regulated in adaptive NK cells
source: This process identified 253 up-regulated and 163 down-regulated genes specific of HBV infection in CHB patients (Fold Change > 2 and adjusted p-value<0.05) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: No significant enrichment was found in the list of down-regulated genes in CHB patient NK cells
source: No significant enrichment was found in the list of down-regulated genes.
evidence: Supported by Metascape analysis results

claim: Analysis of up-regulated genes retrieved Gene annotation terms consistent with ongoing viral infection such as 'Viral life cycle' or 'Hepatitis B'
source: In contrast, analysis of the up-regulated genes retrieved Gene annotation terms that were consistent with ongoing viral infection such as 'Viral life cycle' or 'Hepatitis B' (Figure 4C, a complete version of the analysis is given in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Dysfunctional NK cells up-regulated several canonical genes of the T cell exhaustion program, including LAG3, CD274 (PD-L1), EGR2 and 3, NR4A2, and TOX
source: Moreover, we found that dysfunctional NK cells up-regulated several canonical genes of the T cell exhaustion program, notably immune checkpoints or their ligands, such as LAG3 and CD274 (PD-L1), or transcription factors, such as EGR2 and 3, NR4A2, and TOX (Khan et al., 2019; Seo et al., 2019; Alfei et al., 2019; Scott et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2019; Barber et al., 2006; Williams et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019; Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4D and citations to published studies

claim: Transcripts from exhausted CD8 T cell datasets were strongly enriched in NK cells of CHB patients
source: As depicted in Figure 4E, transcripts of these datasets were indeed strongly enriched in NK cells of CHB patients.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4E

claim: A significant enrichment of the TOX-induced gene signature was detected in genes up-regulated in HBV patients
source: We detected a significant enrichment of this signature in genes up-regulated in HBV patients (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4F

claim: NK cells from CHB patients presented higher expression of TOX
source: As shown in Figure 5A, NK cells from CHB patients presented higher expression of TOX validating the RNAseq data.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Increased TOX expression was seen mainly in the CD56dim subset in CHB patients
source: Increased TOX expression was seen mainly in the CD56dim subset in CHB patients (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: A slight increase in the surface expression of LAG3 was detected in NK cells from CHB patients compared to HD
source: At the protein level, we also detected a slight increase in the surface expression of LAG3 in NK cells from CHB patients compared to HD (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B

claim: LAG3 and TOX protein levels were highly correlated in CHB patients specifically
source: Of note, LAG3 and TOX protein levels were highly correlated in CHB patients specifically, further highlighting their functional link (Figure 5C, R2 = 0.80).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5C

claim: TIGIT was up-regulated in NK cells from CHB patients compared to controls
source: As shown in Figure 5D, TIGIT was up-regulated
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D

claim: TIM3 was down-regulated in NK cells from CHB patients compared to controls
source: while TIM3 was down-regulated
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D

claim: 2B4 expression was unchanged in NK cells from CHB patients compared to controls
source: and 2B4 expression was unchanged in NK cells from CHB patients compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Some CHB patients presented limited but detectable PD1 expression above the average of HD
source: Some CHB patients presented limited but detectable PD1 expression above the average of HD.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D

claim: T-BET was significantly down-regulated in CHB patient NK cells
source: We observed in CHB patients that T-BET was indeed significantly down-regulated, while EOMES was unchanged (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E

claim: EOMES was unchanged in CHB patient NK cells
source: We observed in CHB patients that T-BET was indeed significantly down-regulated, while EOMES was unchanged (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E

claim: The gene set regulated by partnerless NFAT was enriched in NK cells of CHB patients
source: We found that this gene set was enriched in NK cells of CHB patients (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: Ionomycin induced NFAT1 nuclear translocation as soon as 1 hr after stimulation
source: As expected, ionomycin, a Ca2+ ionophore, induced NFAT1 nuclear translocation as soon as 1 hr after stimulation (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Ionomycin treatment increased TOX expression at 4 hr
source: This was followed by an increase in TOX expression at 4 hr (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6C

claim: LAG3 was induced by ionomycin in a way correlated to the expression of TOX
source: Moreover, LAG3 was induced by ionomycin, in a way correlated to the expression of TOX (Figure 6D)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Ionomycin treatment impaired NK cell effector functions
source: As previously published on NK cell lines (Romera-Cárdenas et al., 2016), ionomycin treatment impaired NK cell effector functions (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6E and citation to published study

claim: At a dose of ionomycin of 100 nM, IFN-γ production was completely inhibited while degranulation was still partially conserved
source: Interestingly, at a dose of ionomycin of 100 nM, IFN-γ production was completely inhibited, while degranulation was still partially conserved, a behaviour reminiscent of the functional dichotomy observed in CHB patients.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6E

claim: The production of MIP1-β and TNF-α showed intermediate behaviours in accordance with CHB patients' phenotype after ionomycin treatment
source: The production of MIP1-β and TNF-α showed intermediate behaviours in accordance with CHB patients' phenotype.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Ionomycin treatment at the tested doses was achieved without negative impact on viability
source: This was achieved without negative impact on viability (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by viability measurements (data not shown)

claim: Stimulation of Ca2+ flux in isolation can reproduce key phenotypic and functional features of NK cells observed in a context of CHB infection
source: Overall, these results show that stimulation of Ca2+ flux in isolation can reproduce key phenotypic and functional features of NK cells observed in a context of CHB infection.
evidence: Inferred from the ionomycin treatment experiments showing similar features to CHB patient NK cells

claim: NK cell dysfunction observed in CHB patients is the result of unbalanced Ca2+ signalling
source: These data, in association with transcriptional enrichment of partnerless NFAT-dependent transcripts, strongly suggest that NK cell dysfunction observed in CHB patients is the result of unbalanced Ca2+ signalling.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of transcriptional data and in vitro modeling experiments

claim: Common molecular mechanisms govern T cell exhaustion and NK cell dysfunction in contexts of chronic stimulation
source: This further indicates that common molecular mechanisms govern T cell exhaustion and NK cell dysfunction in contexts of chronic stimulation.
evidence: Inferred from the similarities in transcriptional signatures and molecular features between exhausted T cells and dysfunctional NK cells

claim: Circulating peripheral blood NK cells are largely distinct from liver resident NK cells
source: Since we studied peripheral blood NK cells, a population largely distinct from liver resident NK cells (Marotel et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Marotel et al., 2016

claim: It is unlikely that NK cell dysfunction results from direct stimulation by infected cells
source: it is unlikely that dysfunction results from direct stimulation by infected cells.
evidence: Inferred from the fact that peripheral blood NK cells are distinct from liver resident NK cells

claim: Circulating HB antigen is present in complex with neutralising antibodies
source: Circulating HB antigen is however present in complex with neutralising antibodies (Madalinski et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Madalinski et al., 1991

claim: Immune complexes could chronically stimulate NK cells through CD16 cross-linking
source: These immune complexes could chronically stimulate NK cells through CD16 cross-linking.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the presence of immune complexes

claim: Influenza vaccination increases NK cell function inducing memory-like differentiation based on the sensing of immune complexes by CD16
source: In this respect, it has recently been reported that influenza vaccination increases NK cell function inducing memory-like differentiation (Goodier et al., 2016a). This property is based on the sensing of immune complexes by CD16 (Goodier et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodier et al., 2016a and 2016b

claim: Chronic stimulation of NK cells through CD16 could progressively drive the exhausted signature
source: we can hypothesise that chronic stimulation of NK cells through CD16 progressively drives the exhausted signature seen in our RNAseq.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the CD8 T cell system and observations in the study

claim: A key feature when T cells progress to exhaustion is a defective metabolism and blunted activation of the mTOR pathway
source: A key feature when T cells progress to exhaustion is a defective metabolism and blunted activation of the mTOR pathway, a major coordinator of anabolic and catabolic pathways.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about T cell exhaustion

claim: The decrease in mTOR activity in CHB patient NK cells selectively affected the mTOR pathway since phosphorylation of STAT5 was normal
source: Importantly, this defect selectively affected the mTOR pathway since phosphorylation of STAT5, another signalling event downstream IL-15 Receptor (IL-15R), was normal.
evidence: Supported by data showing normal pSTAT5 levels

claim: Depression in mTOR activity due to chronic activation is reminiscent of the situation in 'non-educated' or 'disarmed' hyporesponsive NK cells
source: Such a depression in mTOR activity due to chronic activation is reminiscent of the situation that prevails in so called 'non-educated' or 'disarmed' hyporesponsive NK cells (Marçais et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marçais et al., 2017

claim: The similarity to disarmed NK cells points towards excessive stimulation of activating receptors as a mechanism
source: Of note, this similarity also points towards excessive stimulation of activating receptors, the mechanism envisaged to explain NK cell disarming (Goodridge et al., 2019; Wu and Raulet, 1997; Johansson et al., 1997).
evidence: Inferred from the similarity to disarmed NK cells and supported by citations

claim: No significant metabolic defect was detected in CHB patient NK cells using several readouts
source: However, we did not detect any significant metabolic defect in CHB patients using several readouts, in contrast to what has been reported for CD8 T cells in CHB patients (Fisicaro et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by data from metabolic assays and citation to Fisicaro et al., 2017

claim: The lack of metabolic defects suggests that exhaustion is at an early stage or that NK cells have a limited capacity to engage a full exhaustion program
source: This finding, associated with the fact that the cytotoxic capacity is spared and that expression of ICPs is low in most patients, suggests either that exhaustion is at an early stage or that, unlike T cells, NK cells have a limited capacity to engage a full exhaustion program, perhaps as a result of a more limited half-life.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observations in the study

claim: A transcriptional signature indicative of improper activation of NFAT transcription factors was detected in dysfunctional NK cells from CHB patients
source: At the molecular level, our results point to a major role of Ca2+ and downstream NFAT signalling in the induction of NK cell dysfunction. Indeed, we detected a transcriptional signature indicative of improper activation of NFAT transcription factors in dysfunctional NK cells from CHB patients.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis showing enrichment of partnerless NFAT-regulated genes

claim: Ionomycin treatment can induce hypo-responsiveness in T cells and NK cell lines
source: Of note, ionomycin treatment also induced hypo-responsiveness in T cells and NK cell lines reinforcing the parallel between both cell types (Romera-Cárdenas et al., 2016; Macián et al., 2002; Dubois et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: In the T cell field, an imbalance in Ca2+ responses is proposed to be the result of defective co-stimulation
source: In the T cell field, such an imbalance is proposed to be the result of defective co-stimulation (Martinez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martinez et al., 2015

claim: Low-grade degranulation could lead to increased concentration of intracellular free Ca2+ and sequential activation of calcineurin and NFAT
source: Since cytotoxic granules are part of the acidic Ca2+ stores, we can hypothesise that low-grade degranulation would lead to increased concentration of intracellular free Ca2+ and sequential activation of calcineurin and NFAT.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the disarming model

claim: In contrast to CHB, disarming does not imprint the transcriptome of circulating NK cells
source: However, in contrast to CHB, disarming does not imprint the transcriptome of circulating NK cells (Goodridge et al., 2019; Guia et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: A combination of signals such as stimulation of activating receptors and increased levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines shapes the NK cell phenotype in CHB patients
source: It is thus likely that a combination of signals such as stimulation of activating receptors and increased levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines (TGF-β and IL-10) (this study and others Peppa et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2012) shapes the NK cell phenotype in CHB patients.
evidence: Inferred from the observations in the study and supported by citations

claim: Targeting the Ca2+ pathway or mechanistically linked molecules could have a positive impact on NK cell effector functions
source: Based on our findings, we would hypothesize that targeting the Ca2+ pathway or mechanistically linked molecules to re-establish a correct signalling balance could have a positive impact on effector functions.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the findings of the study

claim: Ingenol mebutate, an activator of PKCs, was identified for its ability to revert T cell exhaustion
source: In this respect, a recent screen identified ingenol mebutate, an activator of PKCs, for its ability to revert T cell exhaustion (Marro et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marro et al., 2019

claim: Ingenol mebutate was able to complement ionomycin signal for efficient reinvigoration of virus-specific T cells
source: Mechanistically, this compound was able to complement ionomycin signal for efficient reinvigoration of virus-specific T cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Marro et al., 2019

claim: PKC activation could compensate the observed signalling defect and constitute a useful target to restore dysfunctional NK cells activity
source: PKC activation could thus compensate the observed signalling defect and constitute a useful target to restore dysfunctional NK cells activity.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the role of PKCs in signaling

claim: Dysfunctional NK cells of CHB patients present a molecular signature similar to exhausted T cells at the transcriptional and protein level
source: In summary, we provide evidence that dysfunctional NK cells of CHB patients present a molecular signature similar to the one of exhausted T cells at the transcriptional and protein level.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq and protein expression data throughout the study

claim: The molecular signature of dysfunctional NK cells in CHB patients is indicative of a signalling imbalance involving calcium
source: This signature is indicative of a signalling imbalance involving calcium.
evidence: Supported by transcriptional enrichment analysis and in vitro modeling

claim: All patients were diagnosed as inactive carriers according to the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) guidelines for treatment of CHB
source: All patients were diagnosed as inactive carriers according to the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) guidelines for treatment of CHB (European Association for the Study of the Liver. Electronic address: easloffice@easloffice.eu and European Association for the Study of the Liver, 2017).
evidence: Supported by clinical assessment and citation to guidelines
